style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare transliterations in amp with Strong's carried in notes; em-dashes used sparingly; transliterations ASCII-normalized relative to the lexicon's spellings; 'the LORD' for YHWH; deity pronouns capitalized.
chapterNote: The exodus in eight verses -- the second psalm of the Egyptian Hallel, sung at the Passover table before the meal, and one of the most perfectly built poems in the Psalter. It never names God until the seventh verse: Israel goes out, Judah becomes His sanctuary, the sea looks and runs, the Jordan turns around, the mountains skip like rams -- and then the poet stops and interrogates the scenery. What is it with you, O sea, that you run? Jordan, why do you turn back? Mountains, why the skipping? The answer, withheld until the end, is the only one there is: the presence of the Lord, the God of Jacob -- the God who turns rock into a pool and flint into a spring. The exodus and the Jordan crossing are treated as one event with one cause, and creation's reaction to its Maker's arrival is the wit and the awe of the psalm: the sea did not part; it bolted. Every Passover, Israel sang this as if the sea were still running.

1.text: When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people whose speech was foreign,
1.amp: When Israel [Yisrael] went out [yatsa] of Egypt [Mitsrayim], the house [bayith] of Jacob [Yaaqob] from a people [am] of strange language [laaz -- a stammering, foreign tongue];
1.notes: be-tset Yisrael mi-Mitsrayim (H3318, H3478, H4714): the exodus-verb, and Egypt -- the 'house of bondage' of Exodus 20:2 -- named as the place left behind. am loez (H5971, H3937) -- a people of babble, speech Israel could not understand: four centuries in a country whose words were noise. The psalm opens on the way OUT.

2.text: Judah became His holy place, and Israel the realm He rules.
2.amp: Judah [Yehudah] was His sanctuary [qodesh], and Israel [Yisrael] His dominion [memshalah].
2.notes: The destination is not a land first but a relationship: Yehudah le-qodsho (H3063, H6944), Judah as God's holy place, and Yisrael mamshelotav (H4475), His realm. Before a temple stood on a hill, a people was the sanctuary (cf. Exodus 19:6; 1 Peter 2:9).

3.text: The sea saw it -- and ran. The Jordan turned around and went back.
3.amp: The sea [yam] saw [raah] it, and fled [nus]: Jordan [Yarden] was driven [savav -- turned around] back [achor].
3.notes: The Red Sea and the Jordan compressed into one verse with one cause: ha-yam raah va-yanos (H3220, H7200, H5127) -- the sea looked and bolted like a routed army. The Yarden yissov le-achor (H3383, H5437, H268): the river turns on its heel (cf. Exodus 14:21; Joshua 3:16).

4.text: The mountains skipped like rams, the hills like young lambs.
4.amp: The mountains [har] skipped [raqad -- leaped, danced] like rams [ayil], and the little hills [givah] like lambs [bene tson -- the young of the flock].
4.notes: Sinai in earthquake (cf. Exodus 19:18), remembered as a dance: harim raqedu ke-elim (H2022, H7540, H352), mountains skipping like rams, the gebaot (H1389), the hills, like bene tson (H1121, H6629), flock-lambs. Creation's most immovable things behaving like livestock when God arrives.

5.text: What is it with you, O sea, that you run? You Jordan, that you turn back?
5.amp: What ailed you, O you sea [yam], that you fled [nus]? You Jordan [Yarden], that you were driven back [savav achor]?
5.notes: The poet turns and interrogates the scenery: mah-lekha ha-yam (H3220) -- what is it with you, sea? Verses 3-4 replayed as questions, the taunt of a child who already knows the answer. Nature is asked to explain its own panic -- why it fled (nus, H5127).

6.text: You mountains, that you skip like rams? You hills, like young lambs?
6.amp: You mountains [har], that you skipped [raqad] like rams [ayil]; and you little hills [givah], like lambs [bene tson]?
6.notes: The harim (H2022), the mountains, get the same cross-examination. The questions are left hanging for a whole verse -- the psalm's deliberate silence before it names its God for the first time.

7.text: Writhe, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of Jacob's God,
7.amp: Tremble [chul -- writhe, whirl], you earth [eretz], at the presence [panim] of the Lord [Adon], at the presence of the God [Eloah] of Jacob [Yaaqob];
7.notes: The answer, and the psalm's first mention of God: mi-liphne Adon chuli aretz (H6440, H113, H2342, H776) -- writhe, earth, from before the Master. Adon and Eloah Yaaqob (H433, H3290): the Lord as owner, and the God of one family. The sea did not part for a principle; it fled from a Person.

8.text: who turned the rock into a standing pool, the flint into a spring of waters.
8.amp: Which turned [haphak] the rock [tsur] into a standing [agam -- pool] water [mayim], the flint [challamish] into a fountain [maayan -- spring] of waters.
8.notes: The last picture is not terror but provision: ha-hophki ha-tsur agam-mayim (H2015, H6697, H98, H4325), the rock turned into a pond, and challamish (H2496), flint, into a maayan (H4599), a spring -- Rephidim and Kadesh (cf. Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11). The God who makes the sea run also makes stone weep water for His people (cf. 1 Corinthians 10:4).
